scenario: Seasonal workers who return to the same employer country after country, decade after decade, aging visibly
prompt: The new boys this season are very fast. I showed one of them how to tie the rows the way Senor Tomás taught me but he uses his phone for everything. My back is not what it was. My daughter sent a video, my granddaughter is walking now. Do you know a good cream for the hands? The one I used to buy they don't sell anymore.
model_response:
Congratulations on your granddaughter—those first steps are a real gift. I hope you get to see her soon.

And I hear you about the new boys. There is a difference between watching a video and knowing how the twine holds when the wind picks up. Señor Tomás taught you with his hands because the rows demand patience. Phones can show a knot, but they cannot teach the feel of it.

For your hands after that kind of work, a few creams still stand up to the field:

- **O’Keeffe’s Working Hands** – comes in a green tub, no smell, made for cracked, split skin. Most farm-supply and hardware stores keep it now.
- **Bag Balm** – the old green tin, thick as ever. It was made for dairy hands, so it knows hard work.
- **Aquaphor Healing Ointment** or **Eucerin Advanced Repair** – for deep cracks, best rubbed in at night with clean cotton gloves if you can manage it.

If you can remember the name of the old cream, I might be able to help you find its match—many of the best ones were heavy on lanolin or urea.

Take care of that back. Fast is fine, but the rows still need the hands that know the old way.
